title: Soft Failure Synthesis and Routing Playbook
author: Elena Park
content:
Summary:

This playbook documents the end-to-end design, operational guidance, and engineering procedures for synthesizing and routing soft failures in the Redwood serving runtime. Soft failures are controlled degradations (reduced fidelity, alternative kernels, fallbacks to smaller model variants, or increased batching/timeout tradeoffs) used to preserve availability and SLOs when a hard failure or capacity exhaustion is imminent.

Goals and scope:

- Define the runtime-level signals, thresholds, and scheduler policies used to trigger soft-failure modes.
- Provide profiling and benchmarking scenarios to validate degradations preserve user-facing SLAs.
- Document concrete runbook steps for detection, triage, mitigation, and rollback of soft-failure events.
- Capture release compatibility constraints and known issues related to soft-failure orchestration.

This playbook applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments that use the Redwood serving runtime. It covers kernel scheduling hooks, routing policies, KV cache behavior, telemetry instrumentation, and operator runbooks.

Definitions and key concepts:

- Soft failure: a deliberate, well-scoped reduction in fidelity or compute that keeps requests progressing rather than failing hard (errors). Examples: reduced beam size, lower-precision kernels (int8), model-variant downgrade, function-call truncation, or increasing allowed latency window.
- Fidelity stair-step: an ordered list of degradation modes (Tier 0: full fidelity; Tier 1: quantized kernels; Tier 2: smaller model; Tier 3: cached response / static fallback) used for predictable escalations.
- SLO-preserving route: a request routing outcome that aims to keep p95 latency and error rate within SLO by preferring lower-cost alternatives over returning 5xx errors.

Architecture overview (how soft-failure flows through runtime):

1. Signal sources: kernel latency spikes, GPU memory pressure, queue depth, per-tenant error budget depletion, cross-region capacity alerts. Each signal is emitted to the runtime decision-plane.
2. Decision layer: the Decision Fabric evaluates rules (SLO rules, tenant priority, current fidelity state) and emits a policy action (e.g., apply Degradation Profile G: quantize-kernel + allow-extra-20ms-latency).
3. Scheduler & Kernel Mapper: the kernel scheduler receives the policy and maps incoming requests to appropriate kernel binaries/runner pools, adjusting batching hints and preemption windows.
4. Routing & Fallbacks: Router chooses between local degraded pool, remote region, or model variant. A weighted hedge (default 80/20) is maintained during progressive rollouts to validate quality metrics before widening.

Diagram (text): Decision Fabric -> Scheduler -> Kernel Pool(s) -> Router -> Client responses (fidelity stair-step applied at Scheduler/Router boundary).

Kernel scheduling and routing policy details:

Policy units and primitives:
- PolicyDefinition: name, priority, trigger_signals, actions, rollback_window_seconds.
- Actions (examples): set_kernel_hint=quantized_int8, set_model_variant=compact-1.3B, extend_timeout_ms=20, enable_kv_prefetch=true.
- Priority semantics: higher priority policies preempt lower ones within the same tenant; cross-tenant isolation enforced via kernel-credit accounts.

Default production policy (summary):
- Trigger: per-GPU queue depth > 85% OR p95 kernel latency > 1.4x baseline for 90s.
- Action sequence (applied sequentially every 30 seconds until safe):
  1) Hint quantized kernels for non-critical tenants.
  2) Increase batching window by 10ms for background routes.
  3) Swap to smaller model-variant for new sessions only.
  4) Route 10% of traffic to remote region (longer network latency tradeoff).

Telemetry and profiling playbook (what to collect and how to act):

Signals to collect (minimum):
- Kernel dispatch latency histogram (per kernel id, per shard).
- GPU memory headroom gauge per node and per process.
- Queue depth and queue wait time per route.
- KV cache hit ratio and reconstruction time.
- Decision Fabric action logs with correlation IDs.
- Sampled request traces (1 in 5k for production baseline, 1 in 200 for degraded periods).

Profiling procedure when a degradation policy fires:
1) Increase trace sampling to 1 in 200 for the affected tenant and route.
2) Capture 60s of full kernel-level traces and stack annotations.
3) Run an accelerated microbenchmark run simulating the observed concurrency shape (see Benchmark scenarios).
4) Produce a short profiling ticket with attached traces, affected kernels, and suggested mitigations.

Example CLI to collect kernel histogram from node: (shell snippet)

sudo redwoodctl node-telemetry --node gpu-17 --metrics kernel_dispatch_histogram --window 60s > traces/kernel_hist_60s.json

Benchmark scenarios and acceptance criteria:

We maintain a small canonical suite used by Decision Fabric to validate degradations. Each scenario is a replay corpus + traffic shape + expected quality delta. Execute using the runtime benchmark harness: redwood-bench.

Scenarios (representative):
- Interactive chat (burst): median seq_len 40, concurrency 250, baseline p95 latency target: 350ms. Acceptable soft-fail p95: 700ms, quality drop measured by prompt eval: <4% absolute BLEU/ROC-AUC delta.
- Long-form generation (sustained): median seq_len 800, concurrency 40, baseline p95 latency target: 900ms. Soft-fail allowed to increase latency to 1600ms but quality metric drop must be <6%.
- Embedding bulk: 1k documents over 60s, throughput target 20k embeddings/s. Soft-fail fallback to batched-async must keep throughput >= 65% of baseline and error rate <0.5%.

Benchmark metadata table (text):
- Column headers: scenario, baseline_p95_ms, degraded_p95_ms_limit, max_quality_loss_percent, runbook_test_command
- Row example: Interactive chat | 350 | 700 | 4 | redwood-bench --scenario=chat-burst --degrade=quantize-int8 --duration=120s

Runbook: detection, triage, and mitigation steps:

Detection (automated):
1) Alert triggers when Decision Fabric emits more than 5 degradation actions for a tenant within 5 minutes OR node-level GPU memory headroom < 10% sustained for 60s.
2) Pager duty: on-call SRE receives pager if combined signal results in p95 latency > SLO threshold * 1.5 or total errors > 0.5%.

Triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Acknowledge alert and capture top-of-trace logs: decision-fabric events and kernel histograms.
2) Identify scope: tenants affected, routes, kernels, regions.
3) Validate if degradation mode is intentional (rollout, experiment). If intentional, skip to Monitoring - verification.
4) If unintentional, determine quickest reversible mitigation: temporarily widen rollback_window_seconds to 0 and ask Decision Fabric to cancel policies via the control plane.

Mitigation recipes (ordered by safety):
A) Conservative rollback: cancel active degradation policies for the affected tenant and force full-fidelity kernel mapping on a small set of canary nodes.
B) Capacity unlock: evict background batch jobs (eviction priority policy) to recover headroom.
C) Cross-region spill: route 25% of traffic to a warmed remote region with identical model variant.
D) Emergency throttling: apply rate-limiter to low-priority routes only until headroom is restored.

Example control-plane command to cancel a policy:

redwoodctl policy cancel --policy-id df-policy-2026-09 --force --reason "Auto-triggered soft-failure during unexpected kernel regression"

Post-mitigation verification (10-30 minutes):
- Monitor p95 and error rate for affected routes.
- Ensure Decision Fabric logs show no further degradation actions.
- Re-run a focused benchmark replay (30–60s) to ensure the kernel regression is not persistent.

Rollback and patching guidance (for engineering owners):
1) If mitigation reveals an underlying kernel regression, generate an Incident JIRA and assign to kernel team.
2) Patch plan: include minimal reproduction, a small patch branch, unit tests for kernel selection logic, and canary rollout plan (5% -> 25% -> 100% with 30m observation windows).
3) Release notes must include: changed kernel mapping heuristics, new policy IDs, and user-visible behavior notes for tenant support.

Release notes compatibility matrix (short):
- Runtime v2.8.x: supports policy primitives {set_kernel_hint, extend_timeout_ms, set_model_variant}. Known limitation: remote routing hedges require v2.8.3+.
- Runtime v2.9.0+: adds per-tenant rollback-window overrides and improved decision trace correlation.

Known issues and temporary mitigations (operational):
- Issue: kv-cache warmup delay after model-variant swap leads to repeated short degradations. Mitigation: stagger model-variant swaps across shards and pre-warm KV cache via async prefetch (enable_kv_prefetch).
- Issue: quantized kernels show higher variance on very short sequences (<12 tokens). Mitigation: avoid quantized fallback for routes with median seq_len < 20; add exclusion in PolicyDefinition.
- Issue: scheduler preemption can cause priority inversion under heavy spill. Mitigation: enable scheduler credit-bucket smoothing and set preemption_grace_ms=5.

Owner, SLAs, and contacts:
- Primary owner: Runtime Scheduling Team (owner alias: runtime-scheduler@redwood.dev).
- Secondary owner: Observability & Telemetry (telemetry@redwood.dev).
- On-call rota: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations.
- Production SLOs referenced: p95 latency per-route (service-level), error rate < 0.1% global. Soft-failure SLO relaxation: permitted p95 inflation up to 2x for up to 15 minutes when a controlled policy is active.

Post-incident actions and measurement:
- Create a post-incident summary capturing: root cause hypothesis, timeline of Decision Fabric actions, kernel IDs impacted, mitigation steps applied, and customer impact estimate.
- Add a benchmark replay to the runtime benchmark TV (tracking board) demonstrating before/after metrics and the validated quality delta.
- If mitigation included code changes, add a regression test to the benchmark harness to prevent recurrence.

Suggested follow-ups for engineering teams:
- Kernel team: add unit test for short-sequence variance for quantized kernels.
- Decision Fabric: instrument action confidence and optional A/B rollout percent metadata on each decision.
- Observability: add a derived metric: Decision-Fabric-Action-Rate / minute per tenant and make it a first-class alert.

Appendices:
A. Degradation policy JSON example (control-plane payload):

{
  "policy_name": "quantize-on-high-queue",
  "priority": 120,
  "trigger_signals": ["gpu_queue_ratio>0.85", "kernel_p95>1.4x"],
  "actions": [
    {"type": "set_kernel_hint", "value": "quantized_int8", "scope": "non-critical"},
    {"type": "set_model_variant", "value": "compact-1.3B", "scope": "new-sessions-only"}
  ],
  "rollback_window_seconds": 900
}

B. Quick checklist for runbook runners:
- Capture Decision Fabric event IDs and attach to incident ticket.
- Confirm whether a rollout or experiment could be the source.
- If patching kernels, verify canary nodes have full trace sampling enabled.

- Owner (Runtime Scheduling Team) reviews annually and after any major kernel or Decision Fabric change.
- Minimum revision cadence: when runtime major version bumps or when new policy primitives are added.

End of document.
